question: When giving nutrition advice to a patient, what is the main job of a nurse?

options.A: Bridging nutritional science and practical daily meals
options.D: Conducting laboratory tests for micronutrient deficiencies

explanation: You've got this! Nurses act as a friendly bridge, taking big health science ideas and turning them into simple, everyday meal choices that patients can easily manage at home. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h1)

question: Why shouldn't a nurse just hand out a generic diet pamphlet and call it a day?

options.A: Patients refuse to read any written information while admitted
options.B: Dietitians forbid nurses from using printed instructional materials
options.C: Hospital pamphlets are always outdated and medically incorrect
options.D: Patients have unique cultural, financial, and physical backgrounds

explanation: Great thinking! No two patients are the same. Good nursing care means tailoring advice to fit what the patient actually eats, loves, and can afford. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h1)

question: Which ethical principle gives a patient the right to make their own food choices?
explanation: Spot on! Autonomy is all about self-determination—respecting that patients have the final say over their own bodies and choices. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h2)

question: A patient with diabetes keeps sneaking traditional sugary snacks. What is the best first step for the nurse?

options.A: Report the patient to the medical team for non-compliance
options.B: Refuse to provide any further nursing care until they comply
options.C: Remove all personal food items from the bedside table
options.D: Respect their autonomy while calmly explaining the health risks

explanation: You're building great clinical judgment! Instead of policing or scolding, we respect their choice while gently teaching them why health risks matter. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h2)

question: What is measured during an anthropometric assessment?
explanation: Anthropometry involves physical body measurements like height, weight, and body mass index. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h3)

question: You want to find out what a patient ate over the past 24 hours. Which assessment tool should you use?
explanation: Spot on! A 24-hour food recall simply asks the patient to walk you through everything they ate and drank yesterday. It's a quick and easy way to check dietary habits. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h3)

question: What is the main goal of using motivational interviewing with a patient?

options.A: Focusing only on laboratory test results
options.B: Giving the patient a strict list of forbidden foods
options.C: Telling the patient exactly what will happen if they fail
options.D: Helping the patient find their own reasons to change

explanation: Brilliant! Motivational interviewing is about having a supportive chat that helps patients discover their own inner drive to live healthier. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h4)

question: Why are open-ended questions preferred during a dietary interview?

options.A: They encourage the patient to share detailed information
options.B: They guarantee the patient will follow the diet plan
options.C: They take less time to complete than closed questions
options.D: They prevent the patient from asking questions back

explanation: Open-ended questions require more than a simple 'yes' or 'no' answer, opening up a meaningful conversation. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h4)

question: Why do strict, one-size-fits-all meal plans usually fail in real life?

options.A: They are always written in medical jargon patients cannot read
options.B: They contain too many expensive organic ingredients
options.C: They ignore personal preferences and financial realities
options.D: Doctors refuse to let patients follow home meal plans

explanation: Exactly! If a meal plan doesn't match a patient's pocket or favorite local dishes, it's almost impossible for them to keep it up. Keep it realistic! [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h5)

question: A patient loves sweets and is struggling to cut them out completely. What is a smart, gradual first goal?

options.A: Buying expensive sugar-free substitutes from abroad
options.B: Stopping all sugar consumption immediately today
options.C: Replacing sugary snacks with fruit on alternate days
options.D: Ignoring the sweet intake until the next hospital visit

explanation: You're thinking like a pro nurse! Small, baby steps are way easier for patients to stick with than sudden, impossible restrictions. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical challenge when patients try to change their diet?

options.A: Unsupportive family members in the home
options.B: Financial constraints and high food costs
options.C: Excessive availability of free clinical dietitians
options.D: Lack of cooking skills or kitchen facilities

explanation: Correct! Having access to helpful dietitians is a blessing, not a barrier. The real struggles are usually money, time, and kitchen setups. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h6)

question: A patient complains that fresh vegetables are too expensive for their weekly budget. What is the best nursing advice?

options.A: Insist that only imported fresh produce will help their condition
options.B: Suggest nutritious and affordable frozen or local seasonal options
options.C: Advise the patient to borrow money to buy groceries
options.D: Tell the patient to stop eating vegetables altogether

explanation: Wonderful clinical intuition! Always help patients find budget-friendly, local alternatives so they can stay healthy without breaking the bank. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h6)

question: How should a nurse approach dietary counselling with a patient?

options.D: A task completed only upon discharge

explanation: Spot on! Nutrition is a journey, not a one-time lecture. We check in, encourage, and make adjustments as the patient heals. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h7)

question: During a follow-up visit, you notice a patient missed their nutrition goals. What should you do next?

options.A: Discharge the patient from nutrition education
options.B: Reassess barriers and adjust the plan together
options.D: Scold the patient for lack of self-discipline

explanation: You're developing a wonderful bedside manner! Never blame or scold. Team up with the patient to figure out what went wrong and tweak the plan together. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T005#GNS227_U7_T005_h7)
